title: The self alone, before the worlds
hookLine: the Aitareya opens before anything existed: one self, nothing else even blinking, and then a look: let me create worlds
carry: the world comes from the one self
tomorrow: the person; the gods enter through the doors of the body
last: I AM FOOD AND EATER: ONE SELF IN ALL.

lines: WATERS, DARKNESS, AN EGG, A GIANT.
cards: Plenty of old stories about the very beginning start with something already there. Waters. Darkness.
An egg. A giant. The Aitareya Upanishad starts with less.
It belongs to the Rig Veda, the oldest of the four, and it's short, just three chapters. Its first sentence clears the stage: no waters, no darkness, just one thing.
And that one thing does something you might not expect of a lone, perfect being. It thinks. And what it thinks is a sentence of four words in Sanskrit.

teach.b: Here's how it opens: atma va idam eka evagra asit. In the beginning, this was the self, one alone. Nanyat kinchana mishat: nothing else whatever blinked.
Mishat means winking, the tiniest stir of an eye. There was no other eye to blink. Then: sa ikshata.
It looked. It considered. And the thought was: lokan nu srija iti.
Let me create worlds. Not by fighting a monster or splitting an egg. By looking, and wanting.
So the self brings out four worlds, with old, strange names. Ambhas, the waters beyond the sky, with heaven as their floor. Marichi, the rays of light, the middle air.
Mara, the mortal, which is this earth. And below the earth, the waters, apah. Notice the third name.
The world we live on is called, simply, the place where things die. That isn't gloomy. It's accurate, and the next chapters make something beautiful of it.
Notice the order, too. First, a self with nothing to see. Then, seeing.

teach.h: THE WORLDS COME FROM THE ONE SELF.
teach.b: Many Hindu teachers read this as saying the world doesn't come from some second stuff outside the self, but from the self's own looking.
Schools of Vedanta explain that in different ways. But the big teaching fits in one hand: there's no outside to this world.
The worlds, and you in them, come out of the one self, the same self yesterday's singer found on both sides of the plate.

how: The Aitareya is part of the Rig Veda's Aitareya Aranyaka; in traditional Vedic schools it is learned by heart with that Veda, and its opening line is often quoted when teachers explain creation in Vedanta.

games.q: you are the self, one alone. nothing else so much as blinks. what do you do first?
o: look, and think: let me create worlds.
games.why: sa ikshata: it looked, it considered. lokan nu srija iti: let me create worlds. creation starts with a look and a wish.

practice: Close your eyes, let the room go quiet in your mind, and notice what's still here: something aware, before any thought shows up.
When a thought arrives, a sound, a plan, a picture, watch it appear like a small world just made, and let it go. Each one, a little beginning.

wordCard.voice: Atma, the self, alone before anything else. The Aitareya's first line: nothing else blinking, and then a look, and the words, let me create worlds.
